Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about your project needs so we can understand the requirements clearly and support development effectively.

Before we begin, are you in line with the scope of this interview, or do your expectations for this interview differ?

Yes, I’m aligned with the scope. I’m here to talk through the management and reporting needs for PINES, especially around how libraries and consortium staff need to see and use data without affecting normal patron and staff operations.
Thank you. To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to the PINES project?

I’m speaking as a representative stakeholder for PINES, with a focus on library operations and reporting needs across the consortium. I’m familiar with how the shared system is used by branch staff, managers, directors, and consortium administrators, and I can speak to the kinds of information and oversight they need.
Thanks. Could you describe the current process or system you use today for collecting, viewing, and sharing the reporting and management data across PINES libraries?

Right now, a lot of that information is pulled from the integrated library system in separate reports or extracts, and different people end up using different views depending on what they need. Local staff may look at branch-level activity, while managers or consortium folks often have to combine multiple reports to get the bigger picture. It works, but it can be slow and inconsistent, and sharing the data usually takes some manual effort.
What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what features are you hoping to get from this project?

We want to make reporting much easier to access and more consistent across the consortium. It would help if users could quickly view collection use, patron trends, staffing activity, and financial information in a way that supports both local branch decisions and system-wide oversight. We also want to reduce the manual work involved in pulling together reports, so people can spend less time assembling data and more time using it.
Based on your description, do you think a role-based reporting dashboard for different user groups should also be included?

Yes, that sounds like a good fit. Different groups really need different levels of detail, so branch staff, managers, directors, and consortium administrators shouldn’t all see the same thing by default. A role-based dashboard would make it easier for people to get the information they need without exposing unnecessary data.
Could you please elaborate on what you want the role-based dashboard to accomplish?

It should give each user group a fast, clear view of the most relevant operational data for their role, like circulation trends, collection performance, branch capacity, and staff or financial activity where appropriate. For managers and directors, it should also support comparisons across branches and over time, while consortium administrators need broader oversight across all participating libraries. Ideally, it reduces the need to run separate reports just to answer everyday management questions.
Could you describe more about which specific data or measures each role should see, and which of those should be restricted or hidden from certain users?

Branch staff should mostly see day-to-day operational measures for their own location, like circulation, holds, materials handling, and maybe basic patron activity, but not anything that would expose sensitive financial or patron-level detail. Managers and directors should see branch comparisons, collection use, staffing trends, and financial summaries for the branches they oversee, while consortium administrators need the broadest access across all libraries. I’m not fully sure yet where the line should be for patron-identifiable data, so that would need to be verified with policy and privacy requirements.
Are there any other features you would like to see in this project, perhaps something that has not been the primary focus so far?

One thing that would be very useful is export and scheduled distribution, so reports can be emailed or downloaded in a standard format without someone having to recreate them every time. It would also help to have filters for date range, branch, and material type, because that would make the dashboards much more flexible. If possible, some kind of alerts or highlights for unusual activity would be helpful too, but that may depend on what data is reliable enough to track.
Could you prioritize these main features for me: role-based dashboards, export and scheduled distribution, filters, and alerts/highlights?

Role-based dashboards would be the highest priority because that’s the core of making the system useful for different user groups. Next would be filters and export or scheduled distribution, since those are what make the dashboards practical for day-to-day reporting and sharing. Alerts or highlights would be nice to have, but I’d put them last because they feel more optional than the others.
Please elaborate on what you want the role-based dashboards to accomplish.

The dashboards should give each role a quick snapshot of the information they need most often, without making them dig through separate reports. For example, staff should see operational details for their own branch, managers should be able to compare performance across the branches they oversee, and consortium administrators should be able to look across the whole system for trends and exceptions. The idea is to support faster decisions while keeping access aligned with each person’s responsibilities.
Could you describe the current process or system you use today for collecting, viewing, and sharing the reporting and management data across PINES libraries?

Right now, people usually rely on a mix of built-in system reports and manual exports, then share them by email or in meetings. A lot of it is still pieced together by branch staff or managers who need to pull data from different places and combine it themselves. That works, but it takes time and it’s hard to get a consistent picture across all libraries.
Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, and whose needs should we consider, and why?

Branch managers and directors are important because they use the data to make local staffing, collection, and service decisions. Consortium administrators need to be included too, since they care about cross-branch consistency, oversight, and broader system reporting. I’d also include frontline staff, because they understand what information is actually practical to see and use during daily operations.
To help define success, what would you consider a successful deployment of this system for PINES?

A successful deployment would mean people can get the reports and dashboard views they need much faster, with less manual work and fewer one-off spreadsheets. It would also mean the data is trusted enough that managers and administrators actually use it for decisions, not just as a backup source. If it reduces confusion and makes reporting more consistent across branches, I’d consider that a success.

To summarize, we discussed the need for role-based dashboards, filters, export and scheduled distribution, and optional alerts/highlights; access should be aligned by role, with branch staff, managers/directors, and consortium administrators seeing different levels of detail. We also noted that current reporting is still partly manual and inconsistent, and that privacy rules for patron-identifiable data need verification.

Is there anything else you would like to add?

I think that covers the main points well. The only other thing I’d add is that whatever we build should fit into existing workflows without adding much extra training or disruption, because staff are already busy. If there are options for audit trails or usage tracking on reports, that could also be helpful, but I’d want to verify whether that’s really needed.

Thank you for your valuable insights. We’ll follow up with any additional questions or clarifications needed.

Based on our discussion, I will prepare a detailed summary and share it with you for review.
That sounds good. I’m happy to review the summary and clarify anything that comes up.
